subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, July 4, consideration of the motion of Hon. J. L. Ilsley (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Rowe.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I at the outset congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) upon the conciseness and clarity of his budget address. May I also pay a tribute to him for the manner in which he has directed our country's financial policy. It must indeed be a source of great satisfaction to him to know that other nations have adopted these policies which have prevented a vicious spiral of rising prices, otherwise known as inflation. In past wars this has not always been possible. I would remind the house that during the last great war prices rose sharply. Perhaps I could give a few instances. In 1919 flour sold at $7 a bag; to-day it sells for $3.10. Sugar reached 25 cents a pound in 1919; to-day it is only 8 or 9 cents a pound. Butter sold for 80 cents a pound; to-day you can buy it for 38 cents. Eggs cost $1 a dozen; to-day you can buy them in any store for 43 cents a dozen.
Canadians should indeed be proud. Not only have other countries adopted our fiscal

The Budget-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford)
policies and1 our plans for the rehabilitation of our armed forces; they have marvelled at the great industry of our industrial workers and our farmers who have produced such prodigious quantities of war equipment and food. Over and above all this is the crowning glory which comes to us through the gallant deeds of our soldiers, sailors and airmen. The Right Hon. Peter Fraser, speaking in this house on Friday last, paid great tribute to Canada when he said:
The fact that 800,000 men and women have been enrolled in the forces, and the further fact that 2.000,000 persons are taking part in the industrial war effort of this country, are sufficiently eloquent and convincing testimony as to the whole-hearted way in which Canada has thrown itself, without reserve, into what it knew was a struggle for the existence of all that is decent in the life of mankind.
Canada and her allies among the united nations are by nature peace loving people. We were not prepared for war in 1939, and it has taken us four years to attain maximum production. To-day we are geared to a high tempo in war production. It is only natural therefore that there should be few changes m the budget.
The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), whom I should like to congratulate upon being recently elevated to the important post of financial critic of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition-had very little to say of a critical nature with respect to the budget. In one sentence he objected to the abolition of com

pulsory savings on the ground that it would result in lowered financial returns to the government and might start an inflationary trend. Then, in the very next sentence, on behalf of his party he proposed even greater reductions. If a small reduction would cause an inflationary trend, surely a greater reduction would cause a greater inflationary trend. I have never heard anything more inconsistent and more insincere-and this, I may say, from a party that prides itself on total war.

speechtext:
If I said "insincere" I withdraw it, but I did not intend to say it. I believe I used the word "inconsistent".
Let us consider income taxation as it affects those in the lower income brackets. We all feel that we are heavily taxed, but we should not forget that under the proposed budget an unmarried person earning less than 81,100

per year and a married person earning less than 81,600 per year are the lowest taxed persons in the whole civilized world. The proposed changes will affect thousands of girls who are working in factories and as stenographers and clerks in the smaller cities and towns. They will now have deducted just one-half of what was deducted in the past.
A married person with two children making up to $2,000 a year, and a married person without children making up to $1,800 a year, will have only half the deduction that was formerly made. Taxpayers who have not taken allowances for insurance will also find their cheques considerably increased. By the amendment the opposition would abolish certain income taxes, but if you will notice the wording of the amendment you will see that nothing is said as to whether they would abolish compulsory savings.
If the taxpayers are to continue to pay compulsory savings, the amount of reduction in the lower income brackets would be no greater than under the proposed changes in the budget. As I have pointed out, these people are now paying the lowest tax in the world. A single person in Canada earning $800 a year pays less than 87 cents a week, and a married person with two children earning $1,600 pays 51 cents a week. With Canada's income tax for the wage-earner the lowest in the world, does anyone think that a further reduction would raise our prestige with the united nations which may be having greater difficulty in financing than we are? What do you think the boys overseas would say now that the hour of conflict has come for them, now that the hour of battle has arrived when many of them must pay with their lives, if they heard that the people in Canada, who are paying the lowest income tax in the world, were to cease paying taxes altogether? I was impressed by an article in the Brantford Expositor, written by Hal Boyle, Associated Press war columnist, who stated:
The boys overseas have an idea that the people at home still think of the war as a ball game-and that they are enjoying the seventh inning stretch.
It does look like if all the energy being used in fighting the battle of the income tax could be expended on the battle of the Anzio beachhead, Rome would fall in short order.
If I know Canadians, Mr. Speaker, they would resent any further reductions in income tax at the present time. I am confident that they will cheerfully pay the present taxes, which are the lowest amongst the united nations, and are practically nothing when compared with what the boys overseas are paying.

The Budget-Mr. Macdonald (Brentford)
The financial critic of the opposition did not confine himself to finance, but had to advise on military affairs also. He complained about the use or non-use which was being made of our so-called home army. At the outset of his remarks I expected a bold forthright statement of policy on this question, but in that wavering, vacillating, typically Tory fashion he talked all around the subject and said nothing definite. But after all, how can anyone expect anything definite from him, when he gets different leads from different leaders and no lead .at all from one leader? Charles McTague said that the home defence army should all go overseas immediately, while John Bracken, according to a certain section of the press, mumbled a nervous approval, which he has never since confirmed; and during all this time the house leader of the one-time mighty Tory party sits in this house in an uncomfortable silence. I have read and reread the amendment, and the only conclusion that anyone can come to is that the Conservative party would disband the home defence army and send them back to civilian life to pick off all the good civilian jobs before the boys return from overseas, and that is one thing that I will oppose with all my strength. As long as there are good civilian jobs let us retain as many of them as we can for the boys to get when they come home. That is the very least we can do.
I may be asked what I would do with the home army. I would hold them in reserve for reinforcements. They are highly trained and they are an efficient body of men. If our soldiers who recently stormed the shores of Normandy and have now started on their long and arduous trek to Berlin must have reinforcements, these men should and will be sent. Some say that reinforcements will never be needed. I hope they are right, but do not be too sure about it. This war is not yet won. Germany is still a resourceful and a formidable foe. The end may come soon, but we must not take too much for granted.
Suppose it does cost $150,000,000 a year to maintain the home defence force. Is it not far better to spend that large sum of money and win the day than to disband this force and lose everything? Let us not forget that for four years we spent many times $150,000.000 a year to prepare our soldiers to fight in Sicily, in Italy and in France, and if the day comes when the men of the home army should be sent overseas, no one will begrude the cost of their training. If we take the advice of the official opposition in this house and disband this force, and should there not be reinforcements when they are needed, then Canadians for generations to come will hang
their heads in shame. No, Mr. Speaker, this force must not be disbanded. It must be held in reserve to fill the gaps when reinforcements are called for.
While I am referring to the armed forces there are two questions I should like to mention which I trust are not entirely irrelevant to the budget. The first one is with respect to the allowance paid to mothers of men who are serving overseas. At the present time as the house is aware, a dependent mother receives $25 per month, together with $20 assigned pay from her son. She is also allowed to earn $40 from work which she might do. But imagine, Mr. Speaker, an invalid mother trying to live on the magnificent sum of $45 a month. On the other hand, a wife receives $35 a month, together with cost of living bonus, together with a minimum assignment of pay of $23 a month, and an allowance for each child. Personally I could never see why mothers are discriminated against. I understand it is stated that there is a different legal responsibility. I took the time to look over the statutes of the various provinces, and I find that in six of the provinces, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, there are statutes which require a son to support his parents. Section 166 of the Quebec civil code has this wording:
Children are bound to maintain their father, mother or other ascendants who are in want.
In the other provinces I have mentioned the acts are known as the Parents' Maintenance Act, and these statutes state that a son or daughter shall be liable for his or her dependent parents.
I would also draw the attention of the house to section 242 of the criminal code, which makes a man criminally liable if through neglect a parent's health is or is likely to be permanently impaired. So that there is little if any difference legally between the obligation on the part of a son to maintain his mother and the obligation of a husband to maintain his wife. Accordingly I trust that the allowances to mothers and wives will be equalized.
The other matter to which I would refer is the clothing allowance which is given to a soldier when he is discharged. At the present time he is given $65 for that purpose. I am bound to say that I do not think he can clothe himself properly on that amount. How the amount was arrived at I do not know. Recently I visited a number of stores and obtained the prices of clothing. Here are the average prices: Hat, $5.00; cap, S1.75; two shirts, $4.00; B.V.D's, $3.00; socks, $2.25; shoes, $8.00; suit, $35.00; extra working trousers, $7.00 and overcoat, $35.00. amounting in all to $101.00. I have not included a spring

The Budget-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford)
overcoat, overalls, handkerchiefs, et cetera. From these figures I think the house will realize that a man cannot possibly clothe himself on 165. He may possibly get by in the summer, but in the winter, when he has to have an overcoat and other clothing, he cannot buy them unless he receives from $100 to $125. Again I would ask the government to consider raising the clothing allowance, before the snow flies, in any event.
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I revert once again to the budget? There is but one tariff change, and by that change farm implements are placed on the free list. I am somewhat disappointed that not one member of this house who has taken part in this debate so far has concerned himself with the effect that this reduction may have on the workers in these implement factories. Every speaker has either approved the change or has remained silent. I therefore must take it that all parties agree on this tariff change.

One of the foremost policies of the Liberal party is consideration for the men who work in factories, and as long as I have breath in my lungs I shall fight in the interests of these working men.
The tariff has always been a lively controversial issue. The Liberal party, true to its pledge, year in and year out when it has been in power has consistently reduced the tariff.

In fact the Liberal party in its reduction of tariffs has stood against the forces of the world, and its policy has been vindicated by events; the tariff policy of the Prime Minister of this county (Mr. Mackenzie King) is now that of the leaders of the united nations. Every statesman of the united nations has pledged himself to remove tariff barriers. I am in complete accord with that aim. It is not the reduction in the tariff of which I complain but rather the manner or the method by which it was done. The united nations have virtually agreed to reduce tariffs by a multilateral agreement. The farm implement tariff was taken off through no agreement whatsoever with any country; it is the only tariff item affected; and it is for that reason I

Who can tell what the effect will be when there is no shortage of supplies and when all farm implement companies can get all the material that is necessary to turn out these implements?
With the consent of all hon. members there is no doubt that this tariff change will be put into effect. All I can do is to plead with hon. members to see what effect this tariff change will have on the working men in these factories. I ask their sympathetic consideration for these men.

speechtext:
I
much appreciate your remarks, Mr. Speaker, but I may mention that I do not mind a few interruptions.
As I said before, as far as the removal of the tariff on farm' implements is concerned, I have waited all these days for someone to get up and say something on behalf of the workmen in that industry.

The Budget-Mr. Macdonald (Branljord)
I should now like to address myself for a short time to something which I trust is not too far in the future; I refer to the days of reconstruction which will follow the war. The government is now making plans to see that returning warriors and people in the munitions factories are given' employment when the war is over. We must never forget that our soldiers, our sailors and our airmen offered their lives to keep Canada free. They made it possible for us to follow our Canadian way of life, and I trust that we shall make it possible for them to have employment when they return to their homes. I trust also that no member of the armed forces will be discharged against his will from' the forces until he has a job to which he can go. The men and women in the munitions factories must also be provided for; work will have to be found for them too.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has suggested that five billion dollars be set aside for this purpose over the two-year period immediately following the cessation of hostilities. With the principle of that suggestion I ami not at variance; I would however suggest that no limit should be mentioned; whatever amount is necessary to find work for our people should be found. Our government is pledged to that policy. The Prime Minister, speaking last year before the American Federation of Labour, stated that that was the objective wrhich he held most important. The wmrds he used were, "useful employment for all who are willing to work." In other words the government must be responsible for seeing that jobs are provided for all willing workers. No limit, not even five billion dollars in the two year period, should be placed on the amount required for that purpose. Whatever funds are necessary, private funds as well as public funds, must be utilized for that purpose, and whatever jobs are not provided by private industry must be provided by public enterprise.
I would, however, emphasize that large quantities of money will not alone solve our problems of the future. Other nations have obtained large quantities of money by printing press methods, and in every instance it has resulted in national financial disaster, invariably causing great suffering to every man, woman and child in the country concerned. Nevertheless the supply of money can be increased within certain limits. Just what those limits should be no one at the moment can say. We do know, however, that beyond that limit lies national disaster. Our national financing in the years immediately following the war must be directed by men who are bold enough to go forward and cautious enough to
avoid the pitfalls that have invariably brought about financial disaster. The necessity of supplying war materials has taught us much about financing our domestic needs. These lessons we must carry into the peace. The governor of the Bank of Canada and the deputy minister of Finance and their associates have made bold financial strides during the last few years, and I am confident that they will go forward with equal boldness in the years to come. The Minister of Finance has stated publicly that we have learned very much and gone a long way in our development in Canada during the past four years. I join with him in stating that when the war is over we shall turn our financial capacity to the improvement of the Canadian standard of living. Here are his words:
During the war our economic controls and our financial and productive efforts have had to be directed to the destruction of the enemy. We have had to restrict our general standard of living, while protecting that of those near the minimum, in order that we could attain the highest possible standard of fighting. When the war is over, however, we must and will, I believe, turn our economic management, our newly found productive power and our financial capacity to the improvement of the Canadian standard of living. It is then that we shall reap the fruits of the peace we have secured and of the experience which we have gained.
Without doubt the years that are before us will be years of great stress and strain. We need at the helm of all branches of government men of tolerance and experience. The peace conference will not only settle the terms which we shall impose upon our adversaries but will also plan for the future of mankind. There is one statesman in Canada who has far greater knowledge of the intricacies of international law than any other man in this country, and to my mind as great a knowledge as anyone in the world. Recently our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) visited Great Britain and attended the imperial conference, and I believe that members of all parties in this house will join with me when I say that he brought great credit to himself and also to the country of his birth. He alone has an intimate acquaintanceship with the President of the United States and with the Prime Minister of Great Britain. Canada must send her most outstanding statesman to the peace conference, and if the people of Canada will sit down quietly and consider the qualifications and experience of all Canadians, they must come to the conclusion that Canada's representative at the peace conference must be our present Prime Minister.

speechtext:
Before I discuss the budget and the amendment thereto, I wish to say a few words
The Budget-Mr. Green

of encouragement to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). For many years now he has been carrying a great burden, certainly one of the heaviest burdens carried by any man in public life in Canada. At times his work must become very discouraging, and yet I think he should know that from one coast of Canada to the other people admire him for his devotion to duty and for his great sincerity. Personally, while I cannot always agree with the stand he takes-in fact sometimes I think he is rather foolish-I must say I greatly value our personal friendship.
In introducing 'his budget the other day the minister set out that in framing it he had kept in mind four basic considerations. They will be found at page 4174 of Hansard, and are these: The first consideration was the huge cash requirements that must be raised by the Canadian people during the present fiscal year. They amount to in excess of $6 billion, which is nearly $16^ million for every day of the year. He stated that about $2,800 million of that amount would be raised by taxation of one kind or another, and that the balance of over $3,200 million would have to be borrowed from the Canadian people. That of course is a prime consideration. The second consideration he listed was the urgent need for greater production. He described that in the following words:
The second consideration is the urgent need to achieve and maintain the highest possible production of goods and services of which our available working force and management is capable. The urgency of production is very great, and it is immediate. This is not a matter of building up a great organization from which output will flow in one or two years time. The need is for maximum production now- from our present capacity and working force. It cannot be met except by maximum production per person.
The third consideration was the desirability of relieving certain hardships and anomalies in our taxation structure, and the fourth and final basic consideration was given by the minister as the need to prepare for the postwar period. This he expressed as follows:
Finally we have felt it necessary to keep in mind that we are nearer the end of the European phase of the war than we were.
He went on, quite properly I thought, to explain that the war was not yet won, that we were really just getting into the toughest part of the fighting, and then he said:
Nevertheless it is no more than prudent to give sober consideration to some of the problems which will arise when we are able to release some portion of our productive capacity for the purposes of peace.
I thought he might have added a fifth basic consideration, and in the course of his
fMr. Green.]
speech he really did place great emphasis upon it; it was that great reliance is to be placed during the present fiscal year on voluntary support. He mentioned the national war finance committee and praised their work and the support given by the Canadian people, and again I thought he was quite right in doing so. The way the Canadian people have responded to the calls for money has been inspiring. It shows what can be done by Canadians if they direct their energies to the reaching of an objective and work as one united group of people. I really think we could have here what Eric Johnston, the brilliant young president of the United States chamber of commerce has called "America Unlimited". We could have here "Canada Unlimited". We can build this nation into one of the greatest nations of the world. The way in which the Canadian people have responded to the call for funds shows what wonderful things can be accomplished.
After going carefully over the budget speech I came to the conclusion that it was much the same type of speech that might have been delivered toward the end of the first great war, perhaps in the year 1918. It is true that the budget reflects the attitude of the ministry, but I am convinced that it does not reflect the attitude of the Canadian people, that it does not meet present-day. conditions, and that it is not in line with present-day thoughts. Throughout, the speech and the budget overlook the attitude of the ordinary man and woman in Canada, of Mr. and Mrs. Jack Canuck and their family. They are the vast majority of our people; they are Canada. They are the ones who, with a son and perhaps also a daughter in the forces, are doing the war work; they are primarily responsible for the war effort of Canada. These ordinary men and women of Canada are the ones who are buying most of the bonds and obeying the laws and regulations no matter how foolish they think them to be. They are the ones who are getting the telegrams containing messages of death or the information that a loved one is missing.
Mr. and Mrs. Jack Canuck and their family are intelligent, thoughtful, idealistic, courageous, and freedom-loving. They have been doing a lot of thinking in the last few years. They have been through difficult, almost impossible times; they have been through two wars. Every one of them is uneasy at the present time because of the many restrictions on his or her freedom, and is wondering about the post-war years. They are all determined that there must be work for everyone who is willing to work; that there must be reasonable

The Budget-Mr. Green
security for all Canadian people. They are not only asking that preparations be made for the post-war period' but looking for some sign of this fine new world which has been promised to them by so many public men and which they have the right to expect. They are greatly concerned, and I think that most thoughtful members of the house will agree with me-I know that all hon. members are thoughtful-that they are filled with a sense of frustration. Whether this government is to blame for that or not, the fact remains that by and large the Canadian people are filled with a sense of frustration.
Obviously this budget was not drawn with them in mind. It shows no realization of their attitude; it shows no plan to help them to become established in the post-war world and to keep on their feet. There is very little indication that the ministry had that in mind in drawing up this budget. Therefore I make . bold to suggest to the Minister of Finance that he give careful consideration to each paragraph of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) on behalf of the Progressive Conservative party, and to any other suggestions that come out in the course of the debate on the budget or on the budget resolutions. I believe that the amendment moved on behalf of my party more nearly meets present-day conditions than the budget. It is more nearly in line with the thoughts of the ordinary men and women of Canada. I cannot deal to-day with all of the paragraphs of the amendment, but I propose to deal with some of them.
In effect, the first one advocates that adequate steps be taken to simplify the forms and modernize the methods of taxation. At the present time our income tax system is a wonder to behold. Like Topsy in that famous old' book, "Uncle Tom's Cabin," it "jest growed1," and during the war years it has grown faster and in many more directions than it did in years of peace. The position now is such that many people find it extremely difficult to make out income tax returns accurately The good citizen is worried about that. Hi wants to do what is fair by the country; he wants to do his duty, but he finds it almost impossible to make out those new tax returns. The result is that many people have to engage someone to help them, perhaps a lawyer, a notary public or an accountant. People all over Canada are worried about these income tax forms. I realize that some attempt has been made to simplify them, but I suggest to the minister that they must be simplified a great deal more. The Income War Tax Act should be gone over with a fine-tooth comb
and simplified so that the ordinary citizen can make some sense out of it. I find that many of the income tax officers themselves have great difficulty in understanding the provisions of the act; a simplification would be of benefit to them as well as to the ordinary taxpayer.
Then, as to the methods of taxation. Here there is great danger of bureaucracy running wild1; perhaps there is the greatest danger of all to the freedom of the Canadian people in just such things as the methods by which they are taxed. The great majority of our people are honest, even about income taxes; yet some officers-I do not say all the officers, but too many of them in the departments that collect our revenues, treat the people as suspect. A person is treated as a criminal until he proves himself innoeent. It is not a case of the customer being right, but of always being wrong. Some assessors are apt to forget that they are the servants of the Canadian people and not their masters. The great weakness is that at the present time there is no effective check on those government officers; there is n<-effective control over them; hence it is quite possible for bureaucracy to run wild. I have here a letter from a responsible business man in Vancouver carrying on his own business, not in a large way. He complains about the manner in which small firms have been dealt with. He says:
Hundreds-
I will not endorse that. I shall use the word "many" just to be on the safe side.
Many have left the office-
That is the income tax office.
-bullied and insulted, and burning with resentment, with a full knowledge that they were being imposed upon and "gypped". And yet, after a short time, thev paid the assessments so that they could get the worry off their minds and get on with their business, knowing well the difficulties and costs of appeal.

This is in reference to the Vancouver office. The minister may reply that there is provision already for appeals against assessments. It is true there is an appeal, first of all to the Minister of National Revenue, which in effect means to the senior officers of that department, and then the taxpayer may appeal to the exchequer court. But he has to put up $400 as security for costs; he has to incur the expense-of engaging a solicitor; he is let in for all kinds of expenditures, with the result that for Jack Canuck, the ordinary Canadian, there is no appeal. He just decides that it is cheaper not to fight, that he might as well pay, and for the rest of his life or at
The Budget-Mr. Green

least for a very long time he will harbour resentment against the government and against our whole system. This makes it so much harder for him to be a cheerful, willing citizen. I suggest, therefore, to the government that there should be some cheap and summary appeal in cases which do not involve large amounts of money. Perhaps some arrangement might be made for an appeal to the local county court judge. All these county court judges are very highly respected in their districts; they understand conditions, and I believe could very well handle appeals from income tax assessments. You see, Mr. Speaker, the war has caused hundreds of thousands of people to pay income tax for the first time. They have come in contact with the income tax officers, and probably will remain in contact with them for many years to come, during which time the income tax probably will be very heavy and will affect a very large number of the citizens of this country. I cannot stress too strongly the importance of having the Canadian people feel that in these income tax matters they are being treated fairly and that their rights are being preserved.
I propose also to say a few words about the second paragraph of the amendment, which advocates effective action to grant a measure of relief to the men and women in the lower income tax brackets by raising the exemption for single persons to not less than $800 per annum and for married persons to not less than $1,600 per annum. If the exemptions were increased it would help Mr. and Mrs. Jack Canuck, the ordinary men and women of Canada, prepare for the post-war period. The budget makes provision for helping business prepare for that period1. The minister dealt with the matter at page 4174 of Hansard, where he said:
I am concerned only with clearing away some of the uncertainties of fiscal .policy-opening the way for business firms, both large and small, to proceed on as definite as possible a basis with the drawing up of plans for the post-war conversion and expansion of industry and trade on which employment after the war will depend.
I have no quarrel with that, though I think the provisions mentioned by the minister will work mainly to the advantage of large businesses as distinguished from small businesses. It is quite clear that the government is relying upon the individual initiative of business men to provide employment in Canada after the war, rather than upon stateism which of course means the government running everything. I entirely agree with that policy; I think it is right, but I suggest the government should also rely upon and encourage the initiative of Mr. and Mrs. Jack Canuck. The initiative of the individual Canadian is of tremendous value to this country. Sometimes it is very easy

to overlook that fact, but actually Canada was built by the initiative of her people. Canadian troops made their name, both in the last war and in this war, primarily because they displayed as much initiative as any other troops, if not more, and I believe that encouraging the initiative of individual Canadians will result in most of our people being put to work when the war is over; that initiative must not be smothered, as it would be by stateism. At the same time, mind you, it is certainly the duty of any government to prevent unfairness and strictly control monopolies.
There is one way we can help the Canadian people prepare for the post-war period; that is, by increasing these income tax exemptions. Take the men who are being discharged and who will be discharged from the armed forces. Already they number almost 150,000, and more are being discharged at the rate of three or four thousand a month. These men come back and begin to reestablish themselves; at once they are faced with this very heavy income tax, which makes it just that much more difficult for them ever to get a start. Then there is the wage-earner who went through the depression days and has never had a real chance to get back on his feet. There are thousands of office workers, both men and women. There are thousands of small business men; thousands of low salaried men and women; thousands of people working on their own, such as salesmen on commission, taxi proprietors, men doing odd jobs and engaged in many other occupations. By and large these people are the backbone of Canada, and getting them started in the post-war period, encouraging their initiative, is of vital importance to the country. It is not a wise plan to bleed them now, just as we are about to enter the post-war years. Yet in this budget there is no attempt to increase exemptions. The minister has gone the other wTay; he has wiped out compulsory savings. Personally I think it would have been wiser to increase the exemptions, retain the compulsory saving, and to extend the contractual payments allowed as offsets such as premiums on life insurance policies, and principal payments on a mortgage. Those allowances might well have been extended. Perhaps they might have included the payment of other debts, so that many of our Canadian citizens for once in their lives could get out of debt. Consideration might have been given also to providing some offset in connection with the construction of new homes, and so on. If the income tax exemptions had been increased and the compulsory savings retained there would have been very little loss to the treasury during the

The Budget-Mr. Green
war period. I grant that it would have meant repaying compulsory savings after the war, but during these critical times it would have given people a better chance to accumulate something with which to reestablish themselves in the post war years.
The third paragraph of the amendment, to which I wish to refer, is as follows:
(c) This house regrets that no provision has been made to encourage greater war-time production by exempting overtime pay from income tax.
I ask hon. members to remember the second basic consideration of the minister in framing the budget. That was the urgent need for greater production. We must keep in mind the fact that the average Canadian man and woman has been working under great pressure during all the war years. Many Canadians have been doing extra jobs. Men are taking training at nights in the reserve army or are doing A.R.P. work. Many are doing parttime work in the evening after spending all day at their regular jobs. Women are working for the Red Cross and are carrying on innumerable other activities. Our people have been working very hard, and all the time they have been under the constant worry which comes with any war. Our people are weary, and I suggest that when they work overtime the pay they receive should be exempted from taxation. I believe that would help greatly in increasing production until the end of the war.

speechtext:
I do not propose to deal at the present time with paragraphs 4 and 5 of the amendment. One concerns agriculture and the other has to do with our vitally important mining industry; but there will be opportunity to discuss these matters when the budget resolutions are under consideration.
The sixth paragraph reads:
This house regrets that the government has failed to make effective the full mobilization of our financial, industrial and material resources, as well as our man-power, but is maintaining a so-called home-defence army, at a cost to the taxpayer in excess of $150,000,000 per annum, at a time when the need for men for army reinforcements, for farming and for industry is so urgent.
I would like to carry the thoughts of hon. members back to June, 1940. I am sure that
those who were here at that time, and most hon. members were, will remember those terrible dark days. I well remember blue Monday, June 10, when we were informed of the death of the late Norman Rogers, that great friend to all members in the house, who had been killed in such a tragic way. That was the day that Italy struck at France, and our whole civilized world seemed to be falling down about our ears. At that time the house properly passed what was known as the National Resources Mobilization Act, which in effect gave the government of Canada the power to utilize all the resources of the country, both human and material, in whatever way they were needed for the successful prosecution of the war. There was only one exception, that the men called up under the act could not be sent beyond Canada and the territorial waters thereof.
In 1942, almost two years later, we went through another tragic period. This was after Japan had struck and the world again looked very dark. At that time the house passed an act known as the Dominion Plebiscite Act, which provided that a plebiscite should be taken on this question:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service?	[DOT]
A very active campaign followed throughout the country in which members from all sides of the house took part. Advertisements appeared in all papers. I have one here, the main words of which are, "Free Canada for all-out war-vote 'yes.' " Mr. and Mrs. Jack Canuck and their family answered "yes" in no uncertain terms. A majority of over sixty-four per cent of the Canadians who voted, voted "yes." An overwhelming majority voted "yes" in eight of the nine provinces. In three provinces, Prince Edward Island, Ontario and my home province of British Columbia, and in the armed services, the "yes" vote was over eighty per cent, and Nova Scotia and Manitoba were only about one per cent behind that figure.
After that vote the government eventually brought in an amendment to the National Resources Mobilization Act which removed the restriction to which I have just referred, but during the debate on the bill the Prime Minister announced that he would not actually send men called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act overseas without first passing an order in council to that effect and then coming to the house for a vote of confidence. In effect, although the act was changed, the policy remained the same, and that policy continues to this very
The Budget-Mr. Green

day. The whole plebiscite was nothing more or less than a sham, nothing more or less than a fraud on the Canadian people.
What followed was that in some cases the men called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act were persuaded to go active, to enlist for service overseas. That persuasion has consisted sometimes of coaxing, at other times of bluffing, and I am afraid sometimes of bullying. As hon. members know, three divisions were raised for home defence in Canada., the sixth, seventh and eighth. In due course two of those divisions were disbanded and what units remain have for a long time been made up almost entirely of home defence troops, being men who had been called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act. Last year some of those troops were sent as a task force to Kiska and took part in the landing there, Kiska being considered by the government as part of the north American continent. They worked beside United States troops, but when the show was over the Canadian troops were brought back to Canada while the United States troops went on to fight the Japanese in other parts of the Pacific.
This spring the position was that Canada had at home between 60,000 and 70,000 in a home defence army, of whom about 50,000 were in a physical category that would permit them to be sent for service overseas. Most of these were men fully trained in the use of arms, and some of them had been seasoned by taking part in the expedition to Kiska. Right along the government apparently has been afraid to pass the order in council which is necessary in order to permit them to be sent overseas.
A few months ago a campaign was put on by the Pacific command to persuade the home defence troops in that command to go active.
I have here the press clippings of that time which show just what was done. The campaign was under the direction of Major General Pearkes, V.C., one of the outstanding soldiers of Canada, and certainly must have been undertaken with the approval and consent of the Department of National Defence. Genera! Pearkes in his first appeal used these words in speaking to his men:
I regret that we were not allowed to chase the Jap right into his homeland-
Referring to the men who had been to Kiska.
-that time. But that was out of my hands.
I am very proud to tell you that the experience you gained at Kiska makes you invaluable as invasion forces.
The need is urgent. Play the man's part- the part of young Canada.

We ought to be well on the road to victory this year but it will require the assistance and the cooperation of every single one of us.
Then he made this statement to the press:
I tried principally to appeal to their pride in Canada and to the fact that the outcome of the second front might rest upon the number of home defence men who are ready to back up the troops already overseas.
Brigadier Macklin, who was in command of the camp where many of these men were stationed at the time, used these words:
The response to appeals to men to go active has not been satisfactory.
A few days later General Pearkes said this:
No man should wear that khaki uniform unless he is willing to wear it anywhere.
That is what our commander on the Pacific coast thinks of the government's man-power policy. What do the home defence troops themselves have to say? These same dispatches give their attitude. I quote from the Vancouver Sun of April 21:
The men themselves place the blame squarely on the shoulders of the government.
"Why" a number of them asked, "do we have to make the decision? We joined up on being told that we were to receive four months training. That was two years ago. We went to Kiska ready to fight. The fault is not ours. The blame lies on the government policy."
Several weeks later we find this further report:
The main stand taken by non-volunteering home defence troops for failure to go active was that they were quite willing to go under nation-wide conscription, but that they did not see why they should volunteer.
There have been reports submitted by General Pearkes and Brigadier Macklin, and I suggest that the contents of these reports would be very interesting to the house and to the nation if they were made public. I asked the other day f.or the filing of the reports on recruiting, but the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) said that they could not be produced. I think that they would be very helpful in enabling us to find out just what should be done about this question of manpower.
The campaign is still being carried on, and there is no doubt that there either is or will be great need of men overseas. General McNaughton used' these words on June 6, on D-day, just about a month ago. He said:
The call for men for the armed forces is now immediate and insistent.
Brigadier Mess, in charge of recruiting in Canada, on the following day, June 7, is reported as follows:
Speaking of the "vital and urgent need" for "more and more" fighting men to reinforce

The Budget-Mr. St. Laurent
Canada's invasion army. Brigadier James Mess, deputy adjutant-general in charge of recruiting, to-night criticized, several classes of young men who he said were waiting "God knows what for".
I am convinced of two things: first, that our fighting units must be supported at whatever cost; second, that trained and seasoned troops, such as most of these men now in the home defence army are, should be the first sent to reinforce our troops overseas regardless of whether these trained troops are home defence men or volunteers. It just is not good enough to send over half-trained youngsters simply because they have enough public spirit to volunteer. I say that the government's policy is risking a shortage of reinforcements, that it is making all the talk of equality of sacrifice, which was heard on every side when the war broke out, just a mockery in this land. It is creating bad feeling and bitterness between Canadian and Canadian that will last for generations. This man-power policy of the government is not frank, it is not courageous, but it is political. It is an attempt on the part of the government to keep itself in power. It is a policy which effectively prevents any full mobilization of financial, industrial or material resources and of man-power for industry and for the farm. I think it can be fairly described as a disgrace to Canada.
A government that will continue such a policy at this critical time in the nation's history certainly is not fit to lead the Canadian people in the difficult years they are about to face. Mr. and Mrs. Jack Canuck deserve and will demand-and they will get- a government that will give them bold leadership.
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice):	Mr. Speaker, with a number of
arguments which are being used in support of this amendment to the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) that Your Honour do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means I find myself in disagreement, but with respect to most of them I am content to leave the expression of my disagreement to the vote which it will be my privilege to record when the amendment is put to the house.
There is, however, one argument which appears to me to be particularly objectionable and about which I wish to make a few observations. This is what was said by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) on Monday, as reported at page 4435 of Hansard:
I venture to assert, Mr. Speaker, that there are many hon. members sitting in this house who are in favour of the proposals enunciated in the amendment sponsored by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) and who would, if left free, vote for them. That privilege is
denied them and they will perforce be obliged to vote against their convictions and the known views of their constituents. Take the position of hon. members representing industrial ridings. Dare they vote against this amendment? I put it to them to-d-ay. Well, they are on the horns of a dilemma. They must choose here and now. Vote against the amendment and face destruction at the polls, or vote according to the dictates of reason. I challenge hon. members from industrial ridings to vote against this amendment.
I vigorously disagree with the implications of that challenge, both on principle and in respect of the facts which it assumes. I represent an industrial riding, and I am going to vote against the amendment. When the time comes around for an election I intend to go before the' constituents of that riding, if those who supported me in February of 1942 will do me the honour of again selecting me as their candidate, and I do not expect to face destruction. I disagree with the challenge on principle because it appears to me to be destructive of the very basis of British parliamentary institutions. That basic principle was over a century and a half ago stated in eloquent language by Edmund Burke. It has more than once been put upon the records of this house, but I venture to quote it again because I think the lesson should be always present in the minds of hon. gentlemen who sit in this house. I quote:
Certainly, gentlemen, it ought to be the happiness and glory of a representative to live in the strictest union, the closest correspondence and the most unreserved communication with his constituents. Their wishes ought to have great weight with him; their opinion high respect; their business unremitted attention. It is his duty to sacrifice his repose, his pleasures, his satisfactions, to theirs; and above all, ever, and in all cases, to prefer their interest to his own. But, his unbiased opinion, his mature judgment, his enlightened conscience, he ought not to sacrifice to you; to any man, or to any set of men living. These he does not derive from your pleasure; no, nor from the law and the constitution. They are a trust from Providence, for the abuse of which he is deeply -answerable. Your representative owes you, not his industry only, but his judgment; and he betrays, instead of serving you, if he sacrifices it to your opinion.
My worthy colleague says, his will ought to be subservient to yours. If that be all, the thing is innocent. If government were a matter of will upon any side, yours, without question, ought to be superior. But government and legislation are matters of reason and judgment, and not of inclination; and what sort of reason is that, in which the determination precedes the discussion; in which one set of inert deliberate, and another decide; and where those who form the conclusion are perhaps three hundred miles distant from those who hear the arguments?
To deliver an opinion is the right of all men; that of constituents is a weighty and respectable opinion, which -a representative ought always to rejoice to hear; and which he ought always
The Budget-Mr. St. Laurent

most seriously to consider. But authoritative instructions; mandates issued, which the member is bound blindly and implicitly to obey, to vote, and to argue for, though contrary to the clearest conviction of bis judgment and conscience-these are things utterly unknown to the laws of this land, arid which arise from a fundamental mistake of the whole order and tenour of our constitution.
Parliament is not a congress of ambassadors from different and hostile interests; which interests each must maintain, as an agent and advocate, against other agents and advocates; but parliament is a deliberative assembly of one nation, with one interest, that of the whole; where, not local purposes, not local prejudices ought to guide, but the general good, resulting from the general reason of the whole. You choose a member indeed; but when you have chosen him, he is not a member of Bristol, but he is a member of parliament. If the local constituent should have an interest, or should form an hasty opinion, evidently opposite to the real good of the rest of the community, the member for that place ought to be as far, as any other, from any endeavour to give it effect.
That doctrine is particularly wholesome and necessary when parliament is dealing with large issues which affect the very existence and liberty of the body politic. This budget relates to the financing of Canada's part in the great struggle which is being waged at this very moment for the security and freedom of our country as well as for the security and freedom of mankind. This parliament has decided that Canada should take part in that struggle in the fullest possible measure commensurate with its resources. On June 13 I reminded the house of the definition given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) of what we on this side of the house understood to be total war, "the devotion to the prosecution of the war of all the available energies and resources of the nation in excess of those required to maintain the health and efficiency of the people." That policy has been and is being carried out. The total effort of the nation is nothing more than the aggregate of the total efforts of each individual; and just as, for the nation, everything which is not required to maintain the health and efficiency of the population should be devoted to the prosecution of the war, likewise with the individual, all that he does not require to maintain his health and efficiency should be devoted to the pursuance of the object in which his nation is engaged. I quoted again from Hansard, at page 3784, from the same speech of the Prime Minister:
The foundation of the total effort of any country is a correct decision as to the minimum requirements of the civilian population. Once that is determined, production and consumption, except for war, must be steadily and progressively cut down to the minimum. Waste must be eliminated; the manufacture of all luxuries and many comforts must cease. The surplus . . . must be used to make war.

It is the members of parliament who have the responsibility of determining the minimum requirements of the civilian populations and of gauging the extent to which each man can be reasonably called upon to contribute to the national effort. Not only must that effort be made but it must be financed, and each one is also required to do his part, commensurate with his ability to pay, to meet the financial requirements of total war. To suf-gest that any hon. member should be deterred from asking his constituents-all his constituents-to do their part because of fear that he might give offence to some in asking them to do so, seems to me to strike at the very root of hon. members' responsibility to their conscience and to their country.
So much for the principle. I am also in profound disagreement with the assumptions of fact implied in the challenge of the hon. member for York-Sunbury to those in this house whose privilege it is to represent industrial ridings. That challenge places too low an estimate on the intelligence and understanding of the constituents of Quebec East and too low an estimate on the intelligence and understanding of the constituents of other so-called industrial ridings. The pith and substance of that argument is that industrial workers want an exemption from income tax of at least S800 for unmarried men and at least SI,600 for married men; that from their point of view such a raising of the level of exemption is to be preferred to the elimination of the. refundable portion of the income tax as it exists at the present time, and that any failure to support the amendment of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) will constitute a refusal to comply with their desires.
I need not take many words, Mr. Speaker, to remind the house of the true purport and effect of this amendment. The Minister of Finance has moved that you do now leave the chair so that the house may resolve itself into committee of the whole to consider ways and means to finance this year's part of Canada's war effort. The amendment of the hon. member is that the house, instead of going into committee of ways and means to determine how we shall finance this year's portion of our war effort, will content itself with expressing a few regrets-because that is the amendment. The motion is that you leave the chair. The amendment is:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house regrets-
(a) that no adequate steps have been taken to simplify the forms and modernize the methods of taxation;

The Budget-Mr. St. Laurent
(,b) that no effective action has been taken to grant a measure of relief to the men anil women in the lower income brackets by raising the exemption in income tax for single persons to not less than $800 per annum and tor married persons to not less than $1,600 per annum;
(c) that no provision has been made to encourage greater war-time production by exempting overtime pay from income tax."
And so on.
That is the amendment. If that amendment were to be carried by a majority vote of this house, what would be the effect? First of all, it would mean that the financing of the current year's war expenditure would be in accord with the financial provisions which are on the statute books at the present time, and no change would be made. This year, taxes would be paid at the rates provided in the statutes as they exist without any amendment by parliament at this session. Not one penny would be added to the level of exemptions; not one penny would be subtracted from the obligation to pay into the exchequer the refundable portion of the tax; not one penny of relief would be granted on any one of the numerous adjustment provisions covered by the resolutions of the Minister of Finance as placed before the house to be considered when it is in committee. Everything would remain in statu quo.
Let me enumerate some of the things which the resolutions propose to do and which could not be done if the amendment carried; Adjustment of medical expenses allowances; additional expense allowance to the blind; extension of tax credits to include all children dependent on the taxpayer; allowance to persons paying alimony; amendments related to contributions to pension funds; extension of delay of appeal against income tax assessment; consideration to be given to the taxation of annuities and to the succession tax on shares in family corporations; the proposal in respect of the excess profits and corporate income taxes; elimination of customs and war exchange tax on agricultural implements, including cream separators; removal of prohibition against the importation of certain articles-all serious proposals, which the Minister of Finance, in view of his economic survey of the situation, thinks it is desirable to have at this time, but which could not be had if this amendment were to receive the approval of the majority of the members of this house.

You would have all the good things in the budget under a new government. That would be the result.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am just going to deal with what is buzzing in the minds of some hon. members.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: The second effect would be the dismissal from office of the present government and the necessity of holding an immediate general election.

I think you are going to hold it anyway, are you not?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: My hon. friend will ask for further information about that from the leader on this side.
